extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers and contributors: writers, poets, actors, booksellers, and periodical editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative principles for writers, actors, booksellers, and editors as expressed in Spectator essays — covering social precedence, literary reputation, moral purpose of writing, and stylistic/interpretive norms. Useful for producing or evaluating periodical essays, satire, and literary conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial precedence by publication volume
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's place in the Republic of Letters is affected by the amount and form of their published work — 'six Octavo's have at all times been look'd upon as an Equivalent to a Folio' and the author will not 'take place of a Pamphleteer till my daily Papers were gathered into those two first Volumes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary standing may be claimed or recognized on the basis of collected volumes and sustained output; single pamphlets or single octavo works rank below more substantial collected volumes or folios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers' positioning according to authors' merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers and booksellers align themselves relative to one another 'according to the abovementioned Merits of the Authors to whom they respectively belong.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing houses and booksellers will take social and commercial positions based on the perceived merit and reputation of the authors they represent; authors and editors should be mindful that perceived literary merit affects commercial placement and treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedence among learned professions and social rank
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an ordered rank among learned professions and the illiterate classes: the three Learned Professions hold a degree above Squires, who form a lower class — 'this last Order of Men being the illiterate Body of the Nation, are consequently thrown together into a Class below the three Learned Professions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social standing and respectability for writers and intellectuals derive in part from learned status; writers should be aware that learned rank carries social privileges and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage precedence: tragedian over comedian; actresses' rank
rubrics_metrics.description: On the stage social order is observed: 'a Tragedian always takes place of a Comedian' and 'Queens and Heroines preserve their Rank in private Conversation, while those who are Waiting-Women and Maids of Honour upon the Stage, keep their Distance also behind the Scenes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic genre and stage roles carry social significance; actors and playwrights should expect and observe rank distinctions in both public performance and private life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic-genre seating and precedence (tragedy, tragi-comedy, comedy; heroic vs tragic poets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers of tragedy claim precedence in seating/ceremony over comic writers; authors of tragi-comedy take intermediate rank; there is also a historical dispute 'for Precedency between the Tragick and Heroick Poets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genre hierarchies (serious tragedy/heroic poetry above comic or burlesque) inform both critical reception and social treatment; authors should be conscious of these expectations and rivalries when positioning their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of other men's merit (literary patronage and encouragement)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is a very honest Action to be studious to produce other Men's Merit' — the writer/editor should actively promote excellent productions, animate young gentlemen into worthy pursuits, and assist in bringing forth the talents of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and established writers have a duty to encourage, mentor, and publish promising talent; such promotion is both moral and reputationally valuable and is presented as a cultivated virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic writing: please while they cure (gentle moral instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral and corrective writing should be delivered pleasantly: 'Nor harsh thy Precepts, but infused by stealth, Please while they cure, and cheat us into Health.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire and moral instruction should avoid blunt harshness; they succeed best when they entertain while reforming — readers are more likely to accept correction when it is agreeable and artful rather than scolding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretative attentiveness to linguistic and historical nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic lines and diminutives must be read with sensitivity to linguistic usage and context; in discussing Adrian's 'animula vagula' Steele argues that diminutive epithets 'appear not to me as Expressions of Levity, but rather of Endearment and Concern.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreters and critics should consider original language, classical usage, and the likely intent of the author rather than imposing superficial or modern readings that mistake tone or nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary aims: undermine ignorance and substitute learning, piety, and good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The purposeful aim of some writers/editors is to 'undermine the Interests of Ignorance, Vice, and Folly, and attempted to substitute in their Stead, Learning, Piety, and good Sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content should be oriented toward improving the public mind — fostering education, moral virtue, and sound judgment — rather than merely entertaining or pandering to vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivial or profane use of sacred names in discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should refrain from trivializing sacred language: banish 'that prevailing Impiety of using his Name on the most trivial Occasions' and avoid admitting 'so tremendous a Name in the ordinary Expressions of their Anger, Mirth, and most impertinent Passions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone and diction should show reverence where appropriate; casual profanity or frivolous invocations of the divine are judged as impious and unbecoming and damage the moral standing of a piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of affectionate diminutives for intimate, tender tone
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing intimate or dying subjects, diminutive epithets (e.g., 'Vagula, Blandula') express endearment and tenderness rather than levity — a stylistic tool found in Catullus and related poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic choices such as diminutives can deliberately create pathos or tenderness; authors should employ such forms understanding their classical usages and emotive effects.
